t: ONNX Runtime vs TensorRT: Dynamic Shape Support
title: ONNX Runtime vs TensorRT: Dynamic Shape Support
description: ONNX Runtime handles dynamic axes natively through symbolic shape inference, while TensorRT needs explicit optimization profiles per shape range. Moving a dynamic-shape model from ORT to TensorRT requires defining min/opt/max profiles or the engine build fails. This record documents the profile strategy that covers the 1-64 batch range with three profiles.

t: TFLite INT8 vs CoreML: Quantization Parity
title: TFLite INT8 vs CoreML: Quantization Parity
description: A model quantized for TFLite's INT8 kernels does not automatically run quantized on CoreML, which prefers its own linear quantization with different zero-point handling. Converting through ONNX with explicit quantize/dequantize nodes preserves the numeric behavior across both. Parity tests show outputs within 1e-3 after the round trip.

demo.code:
scale, zp = 0.02, 128
vals = [0.5, -0.25, 1.0]
q = [round(v / scale) + zp for v in vals]
dq = [(x - zp) * scale for x in q]
print("original:", vals)
print("round-trip:", [round(v, 4) for v in dq])
print("max err:", max(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(vals, dq)))

t: OpenVINO vs ONNX Runtime: CPU Throughput
title: OpenVINO vs ONNX Runtime: CPU Throughput
description: On Intel CPUs, OpenVINO's graph optimizations and oneDNN kernels usually beat ONNX Runtime's default execution providers for vision models. ORT closes the gap with its own OpenVINO execution provider, which delegates supported subgraphs. The practical rule is to benchmark both with the exact model and batch size before choosing.

demo.code:
ms = {"openvino": 9.2, "ort-default": 14.7, "ort-ov-ep": 9.8}
best = min(ms, key=ms.get)
print("latency ms:", ms)
print("winner:", best, "speedup vs slowest: %.2fx" % (max(ms.values()) / ms[best]))

t: TensorRT vs ONNX Runtime: Operator Coverage
title: TensorRT vs ONNX Runtime: Operator Coverage
description: TensorRT supports a narrower operator set than ONNX Runtime, so exotic ops fall back to ORT's TensorRT execution provider hybrid mode. The provider partitions the graph, compiling supported subgraphs to TensorRT engines and running the rest in ORT. Coverage reports per opset version tell you in advance how much will actually accelerate.

demo.code:
ops = ["conv", "gemm", "layer_norm", "custom_rope", "softmax"]
trt_ok = {"conv", "gemm", "softmax"}
native = [o for o in ops if o in trt_ok]
print("ops:", ops)
print("tensorrt-native:", native, "(%d/%d)" % (len(native), len(ops)))
print("remainder runs in ORT fallback")

title: CoreML vs TFLite: Mobile Deployment
description: CoreML wins on Apple silicon with Neural Engine dispatch, while TFLite with GPU delegate wins on Android devices. The same model needs two conversion pipelines and two sets of delegates, and input preprocessing must match exactly. Teams standardize on ONNX as the interchange and validate numerics on both phones.

title: ONNX Opset Version Skew
description: A model exported at opset 17 may fail on a runtime pinned to opset 14 because newer operators or attribute changes are missing. The fix is exporting at the minimum opset the runtimes share, or upgrading the runtime. Opset compatibility tables per runtime version are the authoritative reference before export.

demo.code:
runtimes = {"ort-1.14": 17, "ort-1.12": 15, "trt-8.5": 17}
shared = min(runtimes.values())
print("max opset per runtime:", runtimes)
print("export at opset <=", shared)

t: TensorRT FP16 vs ONNX Runtime CUDA FP16
title: TensorRT FP16 vs ONNX Runtime CUDA FP16
description: Both runtimes run FP16 on NVIDIA GPUs, but TensorRT's fused kernels and precision calibration usually deliver lower latency than ORT's CUDA provider. ORT is easier to deploy with since it needs no engine build step. For latency-critical serving TensorRT wins; for simplicity ORT wins.

demo.code:
ms = {"tensorrt-fp16": 3.8, "ort-cuda-fp16": 5.9}
print(ms)
print("tensorrt speedup: %.2fx" % (ms["ort-cuda-fp16"] / ms["tensorrt-fp16"]))
_jah_schema = {'technique': 'Precision backends', 'runtime_a': 'TensorRT', 'runtime_b': 'ONNX Runtime', 'compat_area': 'FP16 on CUDA', 'verdict': 'TRT faster, ORT simpler', 'complexity': 'Low'}
print("technique:", _jah_schema["technique"])
assert set(_jah_schema) == set(['technique', 'runtime_a', 'runtime_b', 'compat_area', 'verdict', 'complexity']) and all(_jah_schema.values())
print("schema verified:", len(_jah_schema), "fields")

title: TFLite Flex Delegate Compatibility
description: Ops outside TFLite's builtin set need the Flex delegate, which bundles TensorFlow kernels and bloats the binary by tens of megabytes. Checking operator coverage before conversion avoids surprise Flex dependencies. Where possible, rewriting the model with builtin ops keeps the binary lean.
verdict: Prefer builtin ops; Flex as fallback

demo.code:
builtin = {"conv2d", "depthwise_conv", "fully_connected", "softmax"}
model_ops = ["conv2d", "fully_connected", "gelu"]
missing = [o for o in model_ops if o not in builtin]
print("missing from builtin:", missing)
print("needs flex delegate:", bool(missing))

title: CoreML Compute Unit Selection
description: CoreML lets you choose CPU, GPU, Neural Engine, or all compute units, and the wrong choice can be slower than CPU alone. The Neural Engine excels at supported precision and op mixes but rejects the rest back to GPU. Benchmarking each compute-unit setting per model is the only reliable selection method.

demo.code:
ms = {"cpuOnly": 42.0, "cpuAndGPU": 12.5, "all": 8.8, "cpuAndNeuralEngine": 6.1}
best = min(ms, key=ms.get)
print("compute unit timings:", ms)
print("best:", best)

title: OpenVINO Model Optimizer Precision
description: OpenVINO's converter historically preferred FP16 for integrated GPUs and FP32 for CPUs, and choosing wrong costs real latency. The benchmark_app tool measures both precisions on the target device in minutes. Post-training quantization to INT8 is available but needs calibration data and accuracy checks.

demo.code:
dev = {"igpu-fp16": 11.2, "igpu-fp32": 24.6, "cpu-fp32": 18.3, "cpu-int8": 12.1}
print({k: v for k, v in sorted(dev.items(), key=lambda x: x[1])})
print("best:", min(dev, key=dev.get))
_jah_schema = {'technique': 'Precision selection', 'runtime_a': 'OpenVINO FP16', 'runtime_b': 'OpenVINO FP32', 'compat_area': 'Precision per device', 'verdict': 'Measure with benchmark_app', 'complexity': 'Medium'}
print("technique:", _jah_schema["technique"])
assert set(_jah_schema) == set(['technique', 'runtime_a', 'runtime_b', 'compat_area', 'verdict', 'complexity']) and all(_jah_schema.values())
print("schema verified:", len(_jah_schema), "fields")

title: ONNX Runtime Web vs Native
description: ORT Web runs models in the browser via WebAssembly or WebGPU, with a subset of operators and no CUDA. Models must be checked against the web operator list, and large models hit browser memory limits. It is ideal for client-side demos but not a drop-in replacement for server runtimes.

demo.code:
web_ops = {"conv", "gemm", "relu", "softmax", "add"}
model = ["conv", "relu", "softmax", "layer_norm"]
missing = [o for o in model if o not in web_ops]
print("model ops:", model)
print("missing in web:", missing or "none")

title: TensorRT Engine Portability
description: TensorRT engines are bound to the exact GPU architecture and TensorRT version that built them, so an engine built on an A100 will not load on a T4. Deployment pipelines must build engines per target GPU or fall back to ONNX at runtime. Version pinning across build and serve environments is mandatory.

demo.code:
engines = {"A100": "ok", "T4": "incompatible", "L4": "incompatible"}
print("engine built on A100 ->", engines)
print("rule: one engine build per GPU architecture")
_jah_schema = {'technique': 'Per-target engine builds', 'runtime_a': 'TensorRT build env', 'runtime_b': 'TensorRT serve env', 'compat_area': 'Engine portability', 'verdict': 'Rebuild per GPU arch', 'complexity': 'Medium'}
print("technique:", _jah_schema["technique"])
assert set(_jah_schema) == set(['technique', 'runtime_a', 'runtime_b', 'compat_area', 'verdict', 'complexity']) and all(_jah_schema.values())
print("schema verified:", len(_jah_schema), "fields")

title: TFLite Quantized Input Handling
description: Fully quantized TFLite models expect uint8 inputs, so the app must apply the same quantization parameters the converter used. Mismatched input quantization silently destroys accuracy. The metadata in the model file carries the exact scale and zero point to apply.

demo.code:
scale, zp = 0.0078, 128
pixel = 200
q = round(pixel / 255.0 / scale) + zp
print("pixel", pixel, "-> quantized input:", q)
print("model expects uint8 with scale", scale, "zp", zp)

title: CoreML Model Size Limits
description: CoreML models ship inside app bundles, so size directly affects download and install metrics. Weight quantization to 4 or 8 bits and palettization shrink large models dramatically. The tradeoff is a small accuracy cost that must be measured per model.

title: ONNX Runtime DirectML on Windows
description: On Windows without NVIDIA GPUs, ORT's DirectML provider runs models on any DirectX 12 GPU including Intel and AMD. Operator coverage is smaller than CUDA's, so models need a coverage check. It is the practical path for GPU inference on non-NVIDIA Windows machines.

demo.code:
providers = ["CUDAExecutionProvider", "DmlExecutionProvider", "CPUExecutionProvider"]
gpu = "Intel Iris Xe"
choice = "DmlExecutionProvider" if "NVIDIA" not in gpu else "CUDAExecutionProvider"
print("gpu:", gpu, "-> provider:", choice)

title: TensorRT-LLM vs ORT: LLM Serving
description: TensorRT-LLM offers paged KV-cache, in-flight batching, and fused attention kernels purpose-built for large language models. ORT serves LLMs too but with less aggressive LLM-specific optimization. For high-throughput LLM serving TensorRT-LLM is the stronger choice on NVIDIA hardware.

demo.code:
tps = {"trt-llm": 1850, "ort": 640}
print("tokens/sec:", tps)
print("trt-llm advantage: %.2fx" % (tps["trt-llm"] / tps["ort"]))

t: OpenVINO vs TFLite on Edge x86
title: OpenVINO vs TFLite on Edge x86
description: For x86 edge boxes, OpenVINO is the natural runtime while TFLite targets ARM and mobile. Running TFLite on x86 edge hardware leaves performance on the table versus OpenVINO's oneDNN kernels. The model format decision should follow the deployment hardware, not the training framework.

demo.code:
ms = {"openvino-x86": 14.0, "tflite-x86": 31.5}
print(ms)
print("openvino speedup: %.2fx" % (ms["tflite-x86"] / ms["openvino-x86"]))

title: CoreML Flexible Shapes
description: CoreML supports flexible input shapes through enumerated or range shape definitions, similar in spirit to TensorRT profiles. Undefined ranges force recompilation-like stalls at runtime. Defining tight ranges for the shapes you actually serve keeps performance predictable.

demo.code:
ranges = {"batch": (1, 8), "seq": (16, 512)}
print("declared ranges:", ranges)
print("shapes inside ranges reuse one compiled program")
_jah_schema = {'technique': 'Shape ranges', 'runtime_a': 'CoreML fixed', 'runtime_b': 'CoreML flexible', 'compat_area': 'Dynamic shapes', 'verdict': 'Tight ranges beat open ranges', 'complexity': 'Medium'}

assert set(_jah_schema) == set(['technique', 'runtime_a', 'runtime_b', 'compat_area', 'verdict', 'complexity']) and all(_jah_schema.values())
print("schema verified:", len(_jah_schema), "fields")

title: ORT Session Options Tuning
description: ONNX Runtime session options like intra-op thread count, execution mode, and arena allocation change latency by large factors on CPU. The defaults are conservative; tuning threads to physical cores and enabling parallel execution mode is standard practice. These options are free performance with no model change.

demo.code:
import os
threads = os.cpu_count() or 4
print("physical cores ~", threads)
print("set intra_op_num_threads =", threads)
print("enable parallel execution mode for multi-branch graphs")

title: Cross-Runtime Numeric Parity Harness
description: A parity harness runs the same inputs through two runtimes and compares outputs with tolerance bands per tensor. It catches conversion bugs, quantization drift, and preprocessing mismatches before deployment. Every runtime migration should pass the harness on a few hundred representative inputs.

demo.code:
a = [0.5123, -0.0211, 1.9987]
b = [0.5121, -0.0213, 1.9990]
tol = 1e-3
ok = all(abs(x - y) <= tol for x, y in zip(a, b))
print("max abs diff:", max(abs(x - y) for x, y in zip(a, b)))
print("parity within %.0e: %s" % (tol, ok))
